claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has low hardness.
Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has low strength.
The low hardness and strength are governed by formation of a stable FCC phase.
The stable FCC phase is prone to dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Dislocation-mediated plasticity reduces the alloy's strength.
Dislocation-mediated plasticity reduces the alloy's hardness.
Systematic composition variation can alter phase stability.
Systematic processing variation can alter phase stability.
The intervention will produce a 15% decrease in hardness relative to the starting state.
The intervention will produce a 20% decrease in strength relative to the starting state.
The intervention will increase ductility relative to the starting state.
The proposed mechanism applies at 25 degrees Celsius.
The proposed mechanism applies at strain rates from 10^-3 s^-1 to 10^-1 s^-1.
The applicable composition range is 40-60 at.% of each of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, and Ti.
Failure to observe at least a 10% decrease in both hardness and strength would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe a stable FCC phase would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: An equimolar five-element CoCrFeNiTi alloy would contain about 20 at.% of each element, whereas the stated boundary requires 40-60 at.% of every element. Five concentrations in that range would total 200-300 at.%, so the boundary is compositionally impossible and incompatible with the stated equimolar system.

The starting state's low hardness and strength are attributed to stable FCC, but the intervention merely says to alter phase stability without specifying a direction, while predicting still lower hardness and strength. Altering stability toward or away from FCC would not have a single directional prediction under the stated mechanism.
